messages.author: e7a71d967e60bb41
messages.subject: Histogram with Frequencies
parts:
Dear All,
Sorry for the many emails, but I am a bit stuck with histograms.
I would simply generate a histogram where in each bin I plot the
frequency, i.e. trivially the number of counts in each bin divided by
the overall number of counts...but the code below fails.
Can anyone tell me what I am doing wrong?
Does it have anything to do with this thread

http://tinyurl.com/yd728wr ?

Cheers

Lorenzo

rm(list=ls())
library(ggplot2)


set.seed(1234)
contact <- as.data.frame(rlnorm(10000,1,1.2))
names(contact) <- "contact_data"

gpl <- ggplot(contact,aes(x=contact_data,y=..count../sum(..count..)))+
geom_histogram(binwidth=0.3, colour="darkgreen", fill="white")+
scale_x_continuous(trans = "log10")+
scale_y_continuous(trans = "log10")+
xlab("Contact Duration (sec)")+
ylab("Pairwise Number of Contacts")+
opts(axis.title.x = theme_text(size = 20))+
opts(axis.title.y = theme_text(size = 20, angle=90))+
opts(axis.text.x = theme_text(size=15, colour="gray",vjust=1))+
opts(axis.text.y = theme_text(size=15, colour="gray", hjust=1))


pdf("final_bin_plot.pdf")
print(gpl)
dev.off()

messages.subject: Re: Histogram with Frequencies
parts:
Hi Lorenzo,

The problem is this line:

scale_y_continuous(trans = "log10")

The bar of a histogram runs from ymin = 0 to ymax = count. If you log
transform the y axis, you get ymin = -Inf which does not display well.
It doesn't make sense to log transform the y axis of a histogram.

Hadley

due to my misunderstanding of the problem.

the histogram as having bars running from e.g. ymin=1 (or
1/sum(..count..) if you want to normalize it) to ymax=count?
Then perhaps you would not call that a histogram in the traditional

Any suggested modifications to the code below along the lines I

Cheers

messages.subject: Re: Histogram with Frequencies
parts:
Hi Lorenzo:

There are differences in scale between a frequency histogram and a 'density' histogram.
In the latter, the expectation is that the total area encompassed by the histogram will be
(close to) 1; there is no such restriction in the former. By specifying a density histogram,
you've changed the scale on the vertical axis, in this case to effectively between  0 and 0.8.
Do you really want to represent values in that range on a log scale? That's how you got
the inverted histogram in the first place: it was using log10(1) = 0 as the reference point for
drawing the graph. I'm pretty sure you're not asking for -infinity on the lower end of the
y-scale, right?.  I don't understand your question about 'wanting the y-axis
to stretch high enough to include all my rescaled bins'. Do you want it *just* high enough
or do you want something else? If the former, how do you want the tick values to be spaced?

Note that the shape of the histogram will be the same whether it is a frequency,
percent/relative frequency or density histogram. The only thing that will change is the
representation of values on the vertical axis, and that represents differences in scale.
I'm sure you know this, but we have to be clear about the meaning and representation of
the vertical axis between different manifestations of a histogram.

HTH,
Dennis

tedious, but ggplot2 suits me perfectly for everything else apart from this!


library(ggplot2)

set.seed(1234)
x <- (1-runif(10000))^(-1.5)
x <- x[which(x<=1e5)]

ratio_max <- length(which(x<=10^0.5 & x>= 10^0))/length(x)

messages.author: d674bddd91c6f700
messages.subject: Re: Histogram with Frequencies
parts: I realize this is a very old thread, but I'd like to resurrect it, if only to disagree with Hadley's contention.  It can make perfect sense to plot binned data on a semi-log or log-log scale.  For one thing the binned data in a physics experiment can have an enormous range - you might have billions of counts in some bins and single digits (or zero) counts in other bins.  It doesn't make sense to look at data like that on a linear scale.  Also, physical processes will often give you a distribution of counts that is gaussian or exponential or power law in nature.  Those behaviors are obvious when plotted with the right sort of scale.  Sure, you can't plot log(0), but that's beside the point.

A histogram is both the binning and the representation of those bins
with bars. It can make sense to bin data on a log scale, and then
represent the value of the bins with, say, points. In the lingo of
ggplot, this would be a geom_point with a stat_bin (where geom_bar +
stat_bin = histogram). I think it was the bar, not bin, aspect that was
problematic.
